lead: A cyclic group is built from one element: every element is a power of that generator. Every cyclic group is isomorphic to Z or to Z<sub>n</sub>; these two families are the complete list. This makes modular arithmetic easy to reason about. Cayley's theorem goes further: every group, however abstract, is isomorphic to a group of permutations. The proof uses left multiplication, Lₐ(g)=a·g. These ideas appear in symmetry, coding theory, cryptography and the group algorithms inside computer algebra systems.
prereq: You need: groups and subgroups from 4.2; permutations from Unit 3; bijections from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Take a group G with identity e. The order of G, written |G|, is its number of elements. The order of an element a, written ord(a), is the smallest positive integer n with a<sup>n</sup>=e. If no positive n has a<sup>n</sup> = e, then a has infinite order and we write ord(a) = ∞. In additive notation this is n·a=0. The cyclic subgroup generated by a is ⟨a⟩={a<sup>k</sup> : k∈Z}. If G=⟨a⟩, then G is cyclic and a is a generator. Z under addition is cyclic with generator 1. Z<sub>n</sub> under addition modulo n is cyclic with generator 1. A finite cyclic group of order n is isomorphic to Z<sub>n</sub>; an infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to Z. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic: a subgroup of ⟨a⟩ is ⟨a<sup>m</sup>⟩ for some integer m. Example: in Z<sub>6</sub>, ⟨2⟩={0,2,4}, so ord(2)=3. The group has order 6, the element has order 3. Do not mix these two numbers.

blocks.where: ord(a) is the order of the element a; e is the identity of G; n is a positive integer.

blocks.text: Fix a set X with n elements. A permutation of X is a bijection X→X. The set of all permutations of X under composition is the symmetric group S<sub>n</sub>. It has n! elements. Write a cycle (a<sub>1</sub> a<sub>2</sub> ... a<sub>k</sub>) for the permutation sending a<sub>1</sub>→a<sub>2</sub>, ..., a<sub>k</sub>→a<sub>1</sub>, and fixing other points. Disjoint cycles commute, and every permutation is a product of disjoint cycles. A transposition is a 2-cycle (a b). Every cycle is a product of transpositions: (a<sub>1</sub> ... a<sub>k</sub>)=(a<sub>1</sub> a<sub>k</sub>)...(a<sub>1</sub> a<sub>2</sub>). A permutation is even if it is a product of an even number of transpositions, odd otherwise. Parity is well defined. For n ≥ 2, the even permutations form the alternating group A<sub>n</sub>, a subgroup of S<sub>n</sub> with n!/2 elements. In S<sub>3</sub>, (1 2 3) is even and (1 2) is odd.

Cayley's theorem: every group G is isomorphic to a permutation group. For each a∈G define left multiplication L<sub>a</sub>:G→G by L<sub>a</sub>(g)=a·g. First L<sub>a</sub> is a bijection: its inverse is L<sub>a<sup>-1</sup></sub>, because L<sub>a<sup>-1</sup></sub>(L<sub>a</sub>(g)) = a<sup>-1</sup>(a·g) = (a<sup>-1</sup>a)g = e·g = g. So L<sub>a</sub> is a permutation of the set G. Define φ:G→S<sub>G</sub> by φ(a)=L<sub>a</sub>. For a,b,g∈G, φ(ab)(g)=(ab)g=a(bg)=φ(a)(φ(b)(g)). Thus φ(ab)=φ(a)∘φ(b), so φ is a homomorphism. If φ(a)=φ(b), then L<sub>a</sub>(e)=L<sub>b</sub>(e), so a=b. Thus φ is injective. Therefore G is isomorphic to the image φ(G), which is a subgroup of S<sub>G</sub>. If |G|=n, then S<sub>G</sub> is S<sub>n</sub>. Some syllabi state the theorem as: every group is isomorphic to a permutation group. The image need not be all of S<sub>n</sub>. For Z<sub>3</sub> the image has 3 permutations inside S<sub>3</sub>, which has 6.

blocks.where: φ maps each a in G to the permutation L_a; ∘ is composition; e is the identity; S_G is the permutation group of the set G.

figure.caption: Each row lists a+g mod 3 for g=0,1,2. The three rows are the three permutations L₀, L₁ and L₂; the marked cell shows where 1 sends 0.

spec.title: Left multiplication in Z₃
spec.aria: Three rows show how left multiplication by 0, 1 and 2 permutes the elements 0,1,2 of Z3.

examples.question: Let G=Z₃={0,1,2} under addition modulo 3. (a) Write L₀,L₁,L₂ as permutations of {0,1,2}. (b) Verify Cayley's theorem for G. (c) Find ⟨1⟩ and ord(1).
steps: The three permutations are distinct, so the map a↦L_a is injective. Check one product: L₁∘L₂ sends 0→0, 1→1, 2→2, so L₁∘L₂=L₀=L_{1+2}. Hence it is a homomorphism.
Thus G≅{L₀,L₁,L₂}≤S₃. The image has 3 elements; S₃ has 6.
⟨1⟩={0,1,2}: starting at 0, adding 1 gives 1, then 2, then 0. So ⟨1⟩=G and ord(1)=3.
examples.answer: L₀=(0)(1)(2), L₁=(0 1 2), L₂=(0 2 1); G is isomorphic to {L₀,L₁,L₂}≤S₃; ⟨1⟩=Z₃ and ord(1)=3.
examples.check:
from math import factorial
n = 3
def add(a, b):
    return (a + b) % n
Z = list(range(n))
Ls = [tuple(add(a, g) for g in Z) for a in Z]
print(len(set(Ls)))
s = set()
x = 0
while True:
    s.add(x)
    x = add(x, 1)
    if x == 0:
        break
print(len(s))
x = 0
for k in range(1, 100):
    x = add(x, 1)
    if x == 0:
        print(k)
        break
print(factorial(n))

traps: |G| is the number of elements, while ord(a) is the least positive n with a<sup>n</sup>=e. In Z<sub>6</sub>, |G|=6 but ord(2)=3.
Cayley's theorem says G is isomorphic to a permutation group, not that G is cyclic and not that the image is all of S<sub>n</sub>.
In additive groups an exponent means repeated addition: a<sup>n</sup> becomes n·a, and a<sup>n</sup>=e becomes n·a=0.
Order matters: L<sub>a</sub>(g)=a·g is left multiplication. For nonabelian groups, right multiplication R<sub>a</sub>(g)=g·a is a different map.
Do not call every permutation a transposition; transpositions are only 2-cycles, and parity counts transpositions, not cycles.

quiz.q: Define cyclic group and give one example.
quiz.a: G is cyclic if G=⟨a⟩ for some a∈G; Z₅ under addition is cyclic with generator 1.

quiz.q: Why is every subgroup of a cyclic group cyclic?
quiz.a: If H≤⟨a⟩ and H≠{e}, let m be the smallest positive integer with a<sup>m</sup> ∈ H; then division with remainder shows every element of H is a power of a<sup>m</sup>, so H=⟨a<sup>m</sup>⟩.

quiz.q: In Z₈, list ⟨2⟩ and find ord(2).
Write (1 3 5)(2 4) as a product of transpositions and state its parity.
quiz.a: (1 3 5)(2 4)=(1 5)(1 3)(2 4), a product of 3 transpositions, so it is odd.

quiz.q: Let G be any group of order 4. Cayley embeds G in S₄. Can the image be all of S₄? Explain.
quiz.a: No. |S₄|=24, while the image has |G|=4 elements. Cayley gives a subgroup of size 4, not the whole S₄.

quiz.q: State Cayley's theorem and identify the permutation assigned to a.
quiz.a: Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of S<sub>G</sub>; assign a↦L<sub>a</sub> where L<sub>a</sub>(g)=ag.

quiz.q: In Z₆, compare |G| and ord(2). Is 2 a generator?
quiz.a: |Z₆|=6 and ord(2)=3, so 2 is not a generator; ⟨2⟩={0,2,4}≠Z₆.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cayley's theorem is the starting point of computational group theory: GAP and SageMath store groups as permutation groups. Cayley graphs turn a group into a graph whose edges are multiplication by generators; they appear in network design and expander graphs. In cryptography, cyclic groups such as Z<sub>p</sub><sup>*</sup> and elliptic-curve groups supply the hard discrete logarithm problem behind key exchange. Search for permutation group algorithms, Cayley graph and discrete logarithm.
